lessons.title: Kitchen things

scenes.text: Aarav, 10 months, sits on Amma's hip while she makes breakfast.
Amma holds up a steel spoon: 'Spoon! This is a spoon. Tap, tap, spoon.' Aarav reaches for it.
She peels a banana slowly: 'Banana. Soft, yellow banana.' Aarav laughs and bangs the table.
Tomorrow, when Amma says 'Where is the spoon?', Aarav's eyes turn to it first.

steps.title: Show, name, touch, repeat
steps.body:
Babies learn words by hearing them **many times while looking at the real thing**.

- **Show** the object close to the baby's face (about 20–30 cm away).
- **Name** it in a short, happy sentence: 'Cup! This is a cup.'
- **Touch** – let the baby hold or pat it if it is safe.
- **Repeat** the same word every day. Repetition is not boring to a baby; it is how they learn.
steps.say: Babies learn words by hearing them many times while looking at the real thing. Show the object close to the baby's face (about 20–30 cm away). Name it in a short, happy sentence: 'Cup! This is a cup.' Touch – let the baby hold or pat it if it is safe. Repeat the same word every day. Repetition is not boring to a baby; it is how they learn.

steps.title: Talking while you work
steps.body: Making tea? Say what you see: 'Here is the **cup**. Now the **milk**. Hot! Hot tea is for Amma, not for baby.' Short sentences, one key word, said slowly and clearly.
steps.say: Making tea? Say what you see: 'Here is the cup. Now the milk. Hot! Hot tea is for Amma, not for baby.' Short sentences, one key word, said slowly and clearly.

steps.title: Safety in the kitchen
steps.body: Keep the baby away from the stove, hot liquids, knives and small things like dry chana, peanuts or coins. Only offer clean, large, unbreakable things (a steel bowl, a big spoon) to hold.
steps.say: Keep the baby away from the stove, hot liquids, knives and small things like dry chana, peanuts or coins. Only offer clean, large, unbreakable things (a steel bowl, a big spoon) to hold.

options: Show it once and move on
Show the real thing and say its name many times

scenes.text: Every evening Mei's papa runs a warm bath for her.
'Soap! Bubbles!' he says, rubbing the soap so foam appears. Mei pats the bubbles.
After the bath: 'Towel… pyjamas… teddy… and now, sleepy-time.'
Same words, same order, every night. Mei starts rubbing her eyes when she hears 'teddy'. The words have become her routine.

steps.title: Routines teach words
steps.body: Babies love knowing what comes next. When the **same words come with the same actions** every day (bath → towel → clothes → story → sleep), the baby learns both the words and the routine.
steps.say: Babies love knowing what comes next. When the same words come with the same actions every day (bath → towel → clothes → story → sleep), the baby learns both the words and the routine.

steps.title: Narrate the bath
steps.body: 'Water on your **hands**. Water on your **tummy**. Splash! Here is the **soap**. Now the **towel** – rub, rub, dry!' You are naming objects *and* body parts at the same time.
steps.say: 'Water on your hands. Water on your tummy. Splash! Here is the soap. Now the towel – rub, rub, dry!' You are naming objects and body parts at the same time.

steps.title: Water safety
steps.body: Never leave a baby alone in or near water, not even for a few seconds – a baby can drown in a few centimetres of water. Check the water is warm, not hot, using your elbow or wrist before putting the baby in.
steps.say: Never leave a baby alone in or near water, not even for a few seconds – a baby can drown in a few centimetres of water. Check the water is warm, not hot, using your elbow or wrist before putting the baby in.

quiz.why: The answer is "🧼 Soap". Reason: Soap makes bubbles that clean us. The other choices, such as "🍌 Banana" and "🚌 Bus", do not fit the question. (Question: Which one makes bubbles?)

quiz.why: Babies can drown quickly and silently in very little water. Always stay within arm's reach.

quiz.q: Parent question: why say the same words every bedtime?

quiz.why: Predictable routines comfort babies and give many chances to hear the same words.

scenes.text: Zara, 14 months, rides in a carrier on her grandmother Bibi's chest.
Bibi stops under a big tree: 'Tree! Look up, big tree. Leaves go shh, shh.'
A bird lands nearby. Bibi whispers 'Bird… tweet tweet.' Zara points – her first point at a bird!
On the way home: 'Sun… hot sun. Car… brrm brrm.' Zara tries 'brr!'

steps.title: The world is the best picture book
steps.body: Real things outdoors – trees, birds, dogs, the sun, buses – move, make sounds and change. They hold a baby's attention far better than any screen. Use this app for a few minutes, then go and **find the real thing**.
steps.say: Real things outdoors – trees, birds, dogs, the sun, buses – move, make sounds and change. They hold a baby's attention far better than any screen. Use this app for a few minutes, then go and find the real thing.

steps.title: Pointing is a big step
steps.body: Many babies begin to **point** at interesting things somewhere around 9–14 months. When your baby points, **name what they point at**: 'Yes! A dog!' This is a conversation, even before words.
steps.say: Many babies begin to point at interesting things somewhere around 9–14 months. When your baby points, name what they point at: 'Yes! A dog!' This is a conversation, even before words.

steps.title: Add the sound
steps.body: Pair each thing with a sound or action: car – 'brrm', bird – 'tweet', wind – 'whoosh', rain – 'pitter-patter'. Sounds are often easier for babies to copy than whole words, and they count as early talking.
steps.say: Pair each thing with a sound or action: car – 'brrm', bird – 'tweet', wind – 'whoosh', rain – 'pitter-patter'. Sounds are often easier for babies to copy than whole words, and they count as early talking.

'Sock on one foot… sock on the other foot! Two socks.' Kabir lifts his foot to help.
'Cap on your head!' Kabir pulls it off and laughs. 'Cap off!' says Dadi, laughing too.

steps.title: Dressing is a lesson
steps.body: Each time you dress your baby, name the item and the body part: '**Shirt** over your **head**. **Arm** in, other arm in.' Babies learn clothes words *and* body words together.
steps.say: Each time you dress your baby, name the item and the body part: 'Shirt over your head. Arm in, other arm in.' Babies learn clothes words and body words together.

steps.title: Let them help
steps.body: From around one year, invite the baby to push an arm through or lift a foot. Helping builds coordination and confidence. Expect it to take longer – that is part of learning.
steps.say: From around one year, invite the baby to push an arm through or lift a foot. Helping builds coordination and confidence. Expect it to take longer – that is part of learning.

scenes.text: Whistle! The pressure cooker in Ishaan's Chennai kitchen goes off and 8-month-old Ishaan jumps.
Appa picks him up: 'That's the cooker! Whistle, whistle. Rice is ready.'
Ding-dong – the doorbell. 'Who's that? Doorbell! It's Paati!'
Soon Ishaan turns towards the door whenever the bell rings, smiling.

steps.title: Name the sounds you hear
steps.body: Homes are full of sounds: the cooker whistle, the doorbell, running water, a ringing phone, a fan, a mixer. When a sound happens, **say what it is**: 'That's the phone! Ring ring.' A sudden sound becomes something the baby understands rather than fears.
steps.say: Homes are full of sounds: the cooker whistle, the doorbell, running water, a ringing phone, a fan, a mixer. When a sound happens, say what it is: 'That's the phone! Ring ring.' A sudden sound becomes something the baby understands rather than fears.

steps.title: Babies turn to sounds
steps.body: Many babies turn their head towards a voice or sound by around 4–6 months. Watching for this is an easy, everyday check of hearing.
steps.say: Many babies turn their head towards a voice or sound by around 4–6 months. Watching for this is an easy, everyday check of hearing.

steps.title: Hearing check
steps.body: If your baby does not startle at loud sounds, does not turn towards voices by around 6 months, or is not babbling by about 9–10 months, **ask your paediatrician about a hearing test**. Many hospitals in India offer newborn hearing screening; early help makes a big difference.
steps.say: If your baby does not startle at loud sounds, does not turn towards voices by around 6 months, or is not babbling by about 9–10 months, ask your paediatrician about a hearing test. Many hospitals in India offer newborn hearing screening; early help makes a big difference.

scenes.text: Simran, 16 months, visits her Nani's farm near Ludhiana.
'Moo!' goes the cow. 'Moo!' says Nani. 'Mmm!' tries Simran.
The rooster crows 'Kukdoo-koo!' Simran claps.
Back in the city she points at a goat picture and says 'Meh!' – her very own animal word.

steps.title: Animal sounds are first words
steps.body: Sounds like 'moo', 'baa', 'meow' and 'woof' are easy to say and fun. When a toddler says 'moo' for a cow, that **is a word** – it stands for the animal. Celebrate it and add the name: 'Moo! Yes, a **cow** says moo.'
steps.say: Sounds like 'moo', 'baa', 'meow' and 'woof' are easy to say and fun. When a toddler says 'moo' for a cow, that is a word – it stands for the animal. Celebrate it and add the name: 'Moo! Yes, a cow says moo.'

steps.title: Sounds differ by language
steps.body: In English a rooster says 'cock-a-doodle-doo'; in Hindi and Punjabi often 'kukdoo-koo'; in other languages something else! Use the sounds your family uses – there is no wrong one.
steps.say: In English a rooster says 'cock-a-doodle-doo'; in Hindi and Punjabi often 'kukdoo-koo'; in other languages something else! Use the sounds your family uses – there is no wrong one.

steps.title: Make it a game
steps.body: Hold a toy animal, make its sound, then pause and look at your baby expectantly. That pause invites the baby to 'answer'. This back-and-forth is called **serve and return**.
steps.say: Hold a toy animal, make its sound, then pause and look at your baby expectantly. That pause invites the baby to 'answer'. This back-and-forth is called serve and return.

steps.title: Your face is the first picture book
steps.body: Babies are drawn to faces from birth. Hold your baby face-to-face and show **big, clear expressions**: happy, surprised, sleepy, silly. Name each one.
steps.say: Babies are drawn to faces from birth. Hold your baby face-to-face and show big, clear expressions: happy, surprised, sleepy, silly. Name each one.

steps.title: The social smile
steps.body: Many babies give a real 'social smile' back to a person by around 6–8 weeks. Smile and talk often – your face is teaching them how people connect.
steps.say: Many babies give a real 'social smile' back to a person by around 6–8 weeks. Smile and talk often – your face is teaching them how people connect.

steps.title: Name your baby's feelings
steps.body: When your baby is upset, say what you think they feel: 'You're **hungry**', 'You're **tired**', 'That was **scary**'. Naming feelings while comforting helps children, over years, understand and manage their emotions.
steps.say: When your baby is upset, say what you think they feel: 'You're hungry', 'You're tired', 'That was scary'. Naming feelings while comforting helps children, over years, understand and manage their emotions.

steps.title: You cannot spoil a baby with comfort
steps.body: Responding warmly and quickly to a crying baby builds trust. Babies under one year are not being 'naughty' – crying is how they communicate.
steps.say: Responding warmly and quickly to a crying baby builds trust. Babies under one year are not being 'naughty' – crying is how they communicate.

scenes.text: Yusuf is 5 weeks old. His aunt in Hyderabad makes cards with thick black stripes and circles on white paper.
She holds one about 25 cm from his face. Yusuf stares and stares.
She moves it slowly from side to side; his eyes follow a little.
Months later the game becomes peekaboo – Yusuf giggles every time her face 'comes back'.

steps.title: Why black and white?
steps.body: Newborns see blurry and best at close range (about 20–30 cm). Strong **contrasts** – black on white, bold stripes, checkerboards, simple faces – are easiest for them to see. Colour vision and sharpness improve over the first months.
steps.say: Newborns see blurry and best at close range (about 20–30 cm). Strong contrasts – black on white, bold stripes, checkerboards, simple faces – are easiest for them to see. Colour vision and sharpness improve over the first months.

steps.title: How to play by age
steps.body:
- **0–3 months:** bold black-and-white shapes or your face held close; move slowly side to side to encourage tracking.
- **3–6 months:** brighter colours, a rattle to look at and reach for.
- **6–12 months:** peekaboo, hiding a toy under a cloth, rolling a ball.

Stop when the baby looks away, yawns or fusses – that means 'I need a break'.
steps.say: 0–3 months: bold black-and-white shapes or your face held close; move slowly side to side to encourage tracking. 3–6 months: brighter colours, a rattle to look at and reach for. 6–12 months: peekaboo, hiding a toy under a cloth, rolling a ball. Stop when the baby looks away, yawns or fusses – that means 'I need a break'.

steps.title: Why peekaboo works
steps.body: Peekaboo teaches that things still exist when hidden (**object permanence**), plus turn-taking and anticipation. Babies often enjoy it most in the second half of the first year.
steps.say: Peekaboo teaches that things still exist when hidden (object permanence), plus turn-taking and anticipation. Babies often enjoy it most in the second half of the first year.

scenes.text: In Durban, 7-month-old Sipho says 'ba-ba-ba-ba!' over and over.
His mother answers like it's a conversation: 'Ba-ba! Yes! You're telling me a story?'
At 12 months he says 'ba' every time he sees a banana. Mum says: 'Banana! You want banana!'
That 'ba' is Sipho's first real word – a sound he uses for one thing, every time.

steps.title: The usual journey (ages vary a lot)
steps.body:
- **0–3 months:** cooing (ooh, aah), different cries.
- **4–6 months:** laughing, squealing, playing with sounds.
- **6–10 months:** babbling with consonants – 'ba-ba', 'da-da', 'ma-ma'.
- **Around 12 months:** often a first word or two (it can be a little earlier or later).
- **12–18 months:** slowly more words, lots of pointing and gestures.
- **Around 2 years:** many children put two words together ('more milk', 'Papa go').

Around 12 months: often a first word or two (it can be a little earlier or later). 12–18 months: slowly more words, lots of pointing and gestures. Around 2 years: many children put two words together ('more milk', 'Papa go').

steps.title: How to help: talk *with*, not *at*
steps.body:
- **Copy and expand:** baby says 'ba' → you say 'Banana! A yellow banana.'
- **Pause:** leave a gap so baby can 'reply'.
- **Follow their interest:** talk about what *they* are looking at.
- **Use your home language(s).** Children can learn two or more languages from birth; it does not cause delay.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Correcting harshly ('No, say BA-NA-NA!') – instead, just model the right word happily.
- Background TV all day – it reduces the back-and-forth talk babies need.
- Comparing with other babies – the normal range is wide.

steps.title: When to check with a doctor
steps.body: Speak to your paediatrician if your baby is **not babbling by about 9–10 months**, **not using gestures (pointing, waving) by about 12–15 months**, has **no words by about 16–18 months**, or **loses words or skills they had**. Early support works best.

story.title: Rohan hates tummy time – at first

scenes.text: Rohan, 3 weeks old, cries every time his mother Priya puts him on his tummy.
The nurse at the clinic suggests: 'Try him on your chest first, lying back, face to face.'
On Priya's chest Rohan lifts his head to see her face. Two minutes – then a cuddle.
By 3 months, Rohan pushes up on his forearms on a mat and looks around proudly.

steps.title: What and why
steps.body: **Tummy time** means placing your **awake** baby on their tummy while you watch. It strengthens the neck, shoulders, arms and back – the muscles needed later to roll, sit and crawl – and helps prevent a flat spot on the back of the head.
steps.say: Tummy time means placing your awake baby on their tummy while you watch. It strengthens the neck, shoulders, arms and back – the muscles needed later to roll, sit and crawl – and helps prevent a flat spot on the back of the head.

steps.title: How much?
steps.body: WHO's 2019 guidance for babies under 1 year: be physically active several times a day in many ways, especially floor play, **including at least 30 minutes of tummy time spread across the day while awake** for babies not yet mobile. Start with **1–2 minutes, a few times a day, from the early weeks**, and build up.
steps.say: WHO's 2019 guidance for babies under 1 year: be physically active several times a day in many ways, especially floor play, including at least 30 minutes of tummy time spread across the day while awake for babies not yet mobile. Start with 1–2 minutes, a few times a day, from the early weeks, and build up.

steps.title: Easy ways to start
steps.body:
- On your chest while you lie back.
- Across your lap, with a hand on their back.
- On a firm mat on the floor with a rolled towel under the chest.
- Get down at eye level – your face is the best motivator. Add a mirror or a high-contrast card.

steps.title: Golden safety rules
steps.body:
- Tummy time only when the baby is **awake and watched**.
- For **sleep**, always place babies **on their back**, on a firm flat surface, without pillows, bumpers or soft toys.
- Avoid tummy time right after a big feed if it makes them spit up.

steps.body: Babies learn through all their senses: touch, sight, sound, smell, taste and movement. Sensory play means giving them **safe things to explore** – rough, smooth, cold, warm, soft, hard, heavy, light, noisy, quiet – and **naming** what they feel.

steps.title: The usual order (timing varies)
steps.body:
- **Head control** in the first months.
- **Reaching and grasping** toys (around 3–6 months).
- **Rolling** (often 4–6 months).
- **Sitting** without support (often 6–9 months).
- **Crawling, scooting or bottom-shuffling** (often 7–10 months; some skip it).
- **Pulling to stand, cruising** along furniture, then **walking** (often 9–18 months).

steps.title: How to help

scenes.text: Nikhil is born in Hyderabad. His parents, Swati and Arun, feel thrilled – and anxious about doing everything right.
At 7 weeks, Nikhil looks at Swati's face and smiles back. She cries with happiness.
At 4 months, he pushes up on his elbows in tummy time and laughs when Arun makes silly sounds.
At the 6-month check, the paediatrician asks: 'Does he roll? Reach for toys? Laugh?' Yes, yes, yes.

steps.title: How milestone lists work
steps.body: Milestone lists (such as the CDC's 2022 'Learn the Signs. Act Early.' checklists) describe what **most children (about 3 in 4)** can do by a certain age. So a child who hasn't done something yet is not automatically delayed – but a pattern of missed milestones is worth checking. Count age from the due date ("corrected age") for premature babies, usually until about 2 years.

steps.title: Typical milestones
steps.body:
**By about 2 months:** calms when spoken to or picked up, looks at your face, smiles when you talk or smile, makes sounds other than crying, holds head up briefly on tummy.

**By about 4 months:** smiles to get your attention, chuckles, looks at own hands, holds head steady when held, holds a toy placed in hand, brings hands to mouth, pushes up on elbows on tummy.

**By about 6 months:** laughs, knows familiar people, takes turns making sounds with you, blows 'raspberries', rolls from tummy to back, reaches for a toy, leans on hands when sitting with support.

steps.title: How to help
steps.body:
- Talk, sing and narrate your day; respond to coos as if it's a conversation.
- Lots of supervised tummy time and floor play.
- Give toys to grasp; let baby look in a mirror.
- Respond to crying – you cannot spoil a young baby.

steps.title: Talk to your doctor if, for example…
steps.body:
- No social smile by about 2–3 months.
- Doesn't respond to loud sounds or turn to voices.
- Doesn't follow moving things with eyes, or eyes often cross after 4 months.
- Very stiff or very floppy, can't hold head steady by about 4 months.
- Doesn't reach for things or bring things to mouth by about 6 months.
- **Loses skills** they had.

steps.title: Every child is different
steps.body: General education for parents, not medical advice. **Every child is different** and develops at their own pace. If you are worried about your child's development, health or behaviour, see your paediatrician – early checks and early help work best.

She loves peekaboo and looks for a toy her father hides under a cloth.
'Ma-ma-ma, ba-ba-ba!' she babbles all day.
On her first birthday, she pulls up on the sofa, waves bye-bye and picks up a puffed rice grain between thumb and finger.

steps.title: Typical milestones
steps.body:
**By about 9 months:** may be shy or clingy with strangers, shows several facial expressions, reacts when you leave, lifts arms to be picked up, babbles 'mamama', 'bababa', looks for things dropped out of sight, bangs two things together, sits without support and gets into sitting.

**By about 12 months:** plays games like pat-a-cake, waves bye-bye, calls a parent 'mama/dada' or a special name, understands 'no' (pauses briefly), pulls up to stand, walks holding furniture ('cruising'), picks up small things with thumb and pointer finger (pincer grasp).

steps.title: Stranger and separation anxiety
steps.body: Crying when you leave and wariness of strangers often appear around 8–10 months. It's a **healthy sign of attachment**. Say a short, warm goodbye – don't sneak out – and come back as promised.

steps.title: How to help
steps.body:
- From 6 months, start complementary foods while continuing breastfeeding (WHO advice), letting baby touch and self-feed soft foods.
- Play peekaboo and hide-the-toy.
- Name everything baby points at.
- Childproof the floor – crawling exploration is learning.

steps.title: Talk to your doctor if, for example…
steps.body:
- No babbling by about 9–10 months.
- Doesn't respond to own name by about 9–12 months.
- Can't sit with help by about 9 months.
- No gestures (pointing, waving) and doesn't look where you point by about 12 months.
- Doesn't bear weight on legs with support, or strongly uses only one side of the body.
- Loses skills.

steps.title: Typical milestones
steps.body:
**By about 15 months:** tries 1–2 words besides 'mama/dada', points to ask for something, takes a few steps alone, uses fingers to feed self.

**By about 18 months:** tries to say 3 or more words besides 'mama/dada', follows one-step directions without gestures ('Give me the toy'), walks without holding on, tries to use a spoon, climbs on and off a sofa.

**By about 2 years:** says at least 2 words together ('more milk'), points to things in a book when asked, kicks a ball, runs, eats with a spoon, notices when others are hurt or upset.

steps.title: Tantrums are normal
steps.body: Toddlers feel huge emotions but have few words and little self-control. Tantrums usually peak between about 18 months and 3 years. **Stay calm**, keep them safe, name the feeling ('You're angry the biscuit broke'), don't give in to what caused it, and reconnect afterwards. Hitting or shaming a child does not teach self-control.

steps.title: Boost language
steps.body:
- **Talk more, ask less:** narrate what they are doing.
- **Expand:** child says 'car' → 'Yes, a red car!'
- **Offer choices:** 'Banana or apple?'
- **Read daily** and let them point.

steps.title: Talk to your doctor if, for example…
steps.body:
- Not walking by about 18 months.
- No words, or doesn't point to show you things, by about 16–18 months.
- Doesn't copy actions or words, or doesn't know what familiar things are for (phone, spoon) by about 18 months.
- Not using 2-word phrases by about 2 years.
- Avoids eye contact, doesn't respond to name, or loses words/skills – ask about developmental and autism screening, which is commonly recommended around 18 and 24 months.

steps.title: Your toddler's tantrum
steps.body: Practise a calm response.

a.text: In a supermarket in Pune, your 2-year-old screams and lies on the floor because you said no to chocolate. People stare. What do you do?

choices.label: Stay calm, kneel down, keep them safe and name the feeling: 'You really wanted chocolate. You're upset.'
choices.feedback: Calm naming helps the child's brain settle.

choices.label: Buy the chocolate to stop the noise
choices.feedback: It works now, but teaches that screaming gets chocolate.

choices.label: Shout or smack
choices.feedback: This frightens the child and models hitting; it doesn't build self-control.

b.text: They're still crying, but calmer. What next?

choices.label: Offer a hug and a simple choice: 'Do you want to push the trolley or hold the list?'
choices.feedback: Choices give back a sense of control.

choices.label: Lecture about why chocolate is bad
choices.feedback: Long talks don't land mid-tantrum. Keep it short; talk later.

c.text: Next week, the same tantrum happens – louder. What could you do differently?

choices.label: Hold the limit kindly and calmly, every time
choices.feedback: Consistency makes tantrums shorter over time.

d.text: Your child is now crying harder and scared. What can repair this?

choices.label: Calm down yourself, then hug and say sorry for shouting
choices.feedback: Repair after conflict teaches children too.

end.text: Tantrums pass. Calm limits, named feelings, and reconnecting afterwards help children learn self-control over time.

steps.title: Typical milestones by about 3 years
steps.body:
- Talks with you in conversation with at least two back-and-forth exchanges.
- Asks 'who', 'what', 'where' or 'why' questions.
- Says first name when asked.
- Talks well enough for others to understand most of the time.
- Draws a circle when shown how; avoids touching hot things when warned.
- Notices other children and joins them to play; calms within about 10 minutes after you leave (e.g., at playschool).

steps.title: Pretend play
steps.body: Pretend play – cooking, doctor, shop, superheroes – builds language, planning and empathy. Join in sometimes, but let your child lead.

steps.title: Handling 'why?'
steps.body: Give a short true answer, then turn it back: 'Why do you think the sky gets dark?' Saying 'I don't know – let's find out' is a great answer too.

steps.title: Talk to your doctor if, for example…
steps.body:
- Speech is very hard for family members to understand at 3.
- Doesn't use short sentences, or doesn't understand simple instructions.
- Doesn't play pretend or show interest in other children.
- Falls a lot or has trouble with stairs.
- Loses skills.

steps.title: Typical milestones

**By about 4 years:** pretends to be something else (teacher, superhero), says sentences of 4+ words, names a few colours, tells what comes next in a well-known story, draws a person with 3+ body parts, catches a large ball most of the time.

**By about 5 years:** counts to 10, tells a story with at least two events, follows rules or takes turns in games, hops on one foot, buttons some buttons, writes some letters of their name, answers simple questions about a story.

steps.title: School readiness is more than ABCs
steps.body: Self-care (toilet, eating, dressing), following simple instructions, waiting for a turn, managing feelings and playing with others matter as much as letters and numbers. Formal reading and writing pressure at 3–4 is not needed; play-based learning is recommended in India's **National Education Policy 2020** foundational stage (ages 3–8).

steps.title: Help available in India

- **Rashtriya Bal Swasthya Karyakram (RBSK)** – government screening of children for defects at birth, diseases, deficiencies and developmental delays, with **District Early Intervention Centres (DEICs)** in many districts.
- Speech therapists, occupational therapists, developmental paediatricians and child psychologists.

If you suspect a delay, **don't wait and see** for long – early support changes outcomes.

lessons.title: How much screen time?

scenes.text: In Gurugram, Anita and Vikram give 18-month-old Aarush a phone with cartoons so they can eat in peace.
When they take it away, he screams. He also says fewer words than his cousin.
Their paediatrician explains the guidance and suggests small changes: no screens at meals, more talking, a basket of toys.
Two months later dinner is noisier – but Aarush is chatting and pointing more.

steps.title: What the guidance says
steps.body:
**WHO (2019), children under 5:**
- **Under 1 year:** no screen time.
- **1 year:** sedentary screen time not recommended.
- **2–4 years:** no more than **1 hour a day** – less is better.

**Indian Academy of Pediatrics (2021):** avoid screens under 2 years (except, many experts add, video-calling family); **2–5 years: no more than 1 hour a day**, of good-quality content, watched **with** an adult.

steps.title: Why it matters
steps.body: Young children learn language mainly from **live back-and-forth talk**. Screen time often replaces talking, play, sleep and outdoor activity. Background TV reduces how much parents talk to children. Fast, flashy content and autoplay make it hard for children to stop.

steps.title: A realistic family media plan
steps.body:
- **Screen-free zones:** meals, bedrooms, the car on short trips.
- **Screen-free times:** the hour before bed.
- **Co-view:** watch together, talk about it, connect it to real life.
- **Choose slow, quality content** in your language; turn off autoplay.
- **Model it:** put your own phone away during family time.
- **Video calls with grandparents** are social – they count differently.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Using screens to calm every upset – children then don't learn to calm themselves.
- Screens during meals (linked to overeating and less talk).
- Believing 'educational' apps can replace a talking adult for babies.

steps.title: When to seek help
steps.body: If your child is very distressed without a screen, has delayed speech, poor sleep or little interest in people, talk to your paediatrician.

steps.title: Check your child's day
steps.body: Move the slider to your 3–4-year-old's typical daily screen time.

bands.text: No screens – great, as long as there's plenty of talk and play.

Well above guidance. Make a family media plan and talk to your paediatrician if it's hard to cut down.

lessons.title: Reading aloud so children talk back

scenes.text: In Kolkata, Dadi reads a picture book about a cat to Rimjhim (3) every night.
Instead of only reading the words, she asks: 'What is the cat doing? Where do you think it's going?'
Rimjhim answers: 'Cat go park!' Dadi says: 'Yes! The cat is going to the park to play.'
After a few months, Rimjhim 'reads' the book back to Dadi in her own words.

steps.title: Why read aloud from birth?
steps.body: Reading aloud builds vocabulary, listening, attention, imagination and a bond with you. Babies love your voice and the rhythm of books even before they understand; toddlers learn new words that daily talk doesn't contain.

steps.title: PEER: a simple method
steps.body:
Researchers call talk-rich reading **dialogic reading**. Use **PEER**:

- **P**rompt the child to say something about the book ('What's this?').
- **E**valuate their answer warmly.
- **E**xpand it ('Yes, a big brown dog!').
- **R**epeat the prompt so they try the longer phrase.

Prompts to use: ask them to **complete** a line, **recall** what happened, **open-ended** 'What's happening here?', **wh-questions** (what, where, who), and **distance** – link to their life ('Remember when we saw a cow?').

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body:
- 10–15 minutes daily – bedtime is ideal.
- Let the child choose, even the same book 30 times – repetition is learning.
- Read in your home language(s); any language builds literacy.
- Point to words sometimes, showing that print carries meaning.
- Use voices and sound effects; stop while it's still fun.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- Turning reading into a test ('What letter is this? Wrong!').
- Insisting on finishing every page.
- Only using screens to 'read' stories.

steps.body: Put them in order.

Old magazines and home-made books (photos of the family with captions) work too.

steps.title: Mirrors and windows
steps.body: Children need books that are **mirrors** (characters like them, their language, their family) and **windows** (people, places and lives different from their own).

- **Messy play:** water, mud, dough, paint.
- **Games with rules:** hide-and-seek, simple board games, traditional games like *chain*, *pithu*, *kho-kho* (age-adapted).

courses.summary: Calm, honest, age-right scripts for the questions that make parents freeze: where babies come from, bodies and touching, death, swear words, and why people look different.
outcomes: Parents use a 4-step method: pause, ask what they think, answer short and true, check in
Parents explain where babies come from at a 3–6-year-old level

courses.guardianNote: For parents and carers. Covers where babies come from (non-graphic, age-appropriate scripts based on UNESCO 2018 guidance), children's body curiosity, death and grief, swear words and slurs, and questions about difference. No explicit content.

lessons.title: The method, and 'Where do babies come from?'

scenes.text: In a Chennai supermarket queue, Kavya (4) points at a pregnant woman: 'Amma, how did the baby get in her tummy?'
Her mother, Deepa, wants to disappear. Instead she breathes, smiles and says, 'Great question! What do you think?'
Kavya says, 'Did she eat it?' Deepa laughs: 'No! Babies grow in a special place inside some mothers' bodies called the uterus. Not the tummy where food goes.'
'Oh,' says Kavya, and asks for a biscuit. Deepa realises: a short true answer was enough.

steps.title: The 4-step method
steps.body:
1. **Pause and stay calm.** Your face teaches more than your words. 'That's a great question.'
2. **Ask what they think** ('What do you think?' / 'Where did you hear that?'). You learn what they *really* want to know.
3. **Answer short and true**, at their level, using correct words. You can add more later.
4. **Check in:** 'Does that answer your question? You can always ask me anything.'

It's fine to say: 'Let me think about that and tell you after dinner' – then do.

steps.title: Age-right answers about babies
steps.body:
**Age 2–4:** 'Babies grow in a special place called the **uterus**, inside the mother's body, below her tummy.'

**Age 4–6, if they ask how it starts:** 'To make a baby, a tiny **egg** from a woman's body and a tiny **sperm** from a man's body join together. Then the baby slowly grows in the uterus for about nine months.'

**How it comes out:** 'Usually through an opening called the **vagina**, which stretches. Sometimes doctors help the baby out with an operation called a **caesarean**.'

Families are also made through adoption, and some babies start with doctors' help (like IVF) – you can mention this if it fits your family.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- **Myths** ('stork', 'from the hospital', 'God put it there') – children later feel misled and stop asking you.
- **Over-answering** with far more detail than asked.
- **Shaming** ('Chee! Don't ask that!') – this teaches that bodies are dirty and you're not safe to ask, which leaves children vulnerable to wrong information and to abuse.

Children with correct, calm information are **better protected**, not 'spoiled'. This is the approach of UNESCO's 2018 guidance.

steps.title: Keep the door open
steps.body: You will have this talk many times as they grow, a little deeper each time. The goal is not one perfect talk; it's being **the person they come to**.

steps.body: Open each question and read a sample answer aloud.

items.a: 'You grew in a special place inside me called the uterus. It's near my tummy but it's not where food goes.' (If adopted: 'You grew inside your birth mother's uterus, and then you came to our family.')

'Most babies come out through an opening between the mother's legs called the vagina – it stretches. Some babies come out through a cut the doctor makes in the mother's belly; it's called a caesarean.'
'Babies grow in a uterus. Most girls are born with a uterus and most boys are not. Both men and women are needed to start a baby – a sperm and an egg.'

items.a: A simple, non-graphic answer: 'When grown-ups decide to have a baby, the sperm comes from the man's penis into the woman's vagina, and swims to the egg. This is something for grown-up bodies only.' Many parents give this answer only if the child keeps asking; it is fine to say 'That's a good question, and I'll tell you more when you're a bit older.'
'She has a baby growing inside her uterus. It will be born in a few months.' Also teach: it's polite not to point or comment on people's bodies loudly.

scenes.text: In Pune, Arjun (4) asks during his bath, 'Why does Didi not have a penis?'
His father answers simply: 'Boys usually have a penis and girls usually have a vulva. Different bodies, both normal.'
A week later, Arjun's grandmother sees him touching his penis while watching TV and gasps.
His father calmly tells Arjun, 'Touching your private parts is something we do only in private, like in your room or the bathroom.' Arjun goes back to his blocks.

steps.title: Curiosity is normal
steps.body: Young children are naturally curious about their own and others' bodies: they ask about differences, want to see, play 'doctor', and many touch their own genitals because it feels soothing. **This is a normal part of development** in young children.

steps.title: What to say
steps.body:
- **Differences:** 'Boys usually have a penis and testicles; girls usually have a vulva and vagina. Everyone's body is a little different.'
- **Self-touch:** calmly teach **privacy** ('That's for private places, like your bedroom') and redirect – no shaming, no punishment.
- **Nudity at home:** each family decides; as children grow, teach knocking, closing doors and privacy for themselves and others.

steps.title: Playing 'doctor' with other children
steps.body: Mutual curiosity between children of a **similar age and size** who play willingly happens and is usually not a concern. Calmly stop it, redirect, and use it to teach the **body rules**: private parts are private, we don't touch other people's private parts or ask them to touch ours, and anyone can say no.

steps.title: When to seek advice
steps.body: Talk to your paediatrician or a child psychologist if sexual behaviour is **frequent and hard to redirect**, involves **coercion, force or a big age gap**, causes **distress**, imitates adult sexual acts, or if a child shows knowledge beyond their age. These can be signs that a child has been exposed to sexual content or abuse. In India, **Childline 1098** and **112** can help.

steps.title: Usually typical, or seek advice?
steps.body: Sort these behaviours in 3–6-year-olds.

lessons.title: 'Where did Dadaji go?' – talking about death

scenes.text: In Varanasi, Pihu (5)'s grandfather dies. Everyone is crying. Someone tells her, 'Dadaji has gone to sleep forever.'
That night Pihu refuses to sleep. 'What if I don't wake up too?'
Her mother sits with her: 'Dadaji died. His body stopped working, and it can't start again. He doesn't feel pain or cold. Sleeping is different – when we sleep, we wake up.'
Together they put marigolds by Dadaji's chair and talk about his funny stories.

steps.title: How young children understand death
steps.body: Under about 5–7, many children don't yet understand that death is **permanent**, **happens to all living things**, and means the **body stops working completely**. They may ask the same questions many times, or seem fine and then play 'funeral'. This is how they process it.

steps.title: Use clear words
steps.body:
Say **'died'** and **'dead'**, not 'sleeping', 'lost', or 'gone away' – these can cause fear of sleep or of being left. For example:

*'Dadaji died. His body stopped working – his heart stopped beating and he stopped breathing. He can't feel pain anymore. He won't come back, and we will miss him.'*

Then share your family's beliefs (heaven, rebirth, the soul, or none) as **your family's beliefs** – children can hold both the biological fact and your faith.

steps.title: Questions they ask
steps.body:
- **'Will you die?'** – 'Most people die when they are very, very old. I plan to be here for a long, long time to look after you.'
- **'Did I make it happen?'** – 'No. Nothing you thought, said or did made Dadaji die.'
- **'Can I come to the funeral?'** – Many children benefit from being included, with preparation and a trusted adult beside them.

steps.title: When to get help
steps.body: Grief in children can show as clinginess, tantrums, bedwetting, sleep problems or tummy aches. If these are severe or last many weeks, or your child talks about wanting to die to be with the person, speak to your paediatrician or a child counsellor. Tele-MANAS (**14416**) offers free mental-health support in India, including for grieving parents.

steps.title: Practise
steps.body: Choose what to say.

a.text: Your 4-year-old's pet fish has died. She asks, 'Why isn't Goldie swimming?' What do you say?

choices.label: 'Goldie died. Her body stopped working, so she can't swim or eat anymore.'
choices.feedback: Clear and gentle.

choices.label: 'Goldie is sleeping.'
choices.feedback: This can make her afraid of sleep, or wait for Goldie to wake.

choices.label: Flush it and buy an identical fish secretly
choices.feedback: Children often notice, and it misses a chance to learn about loss.

c.text: Your child seems confused and keeps asking when Goldie will wake up. What now?

choices.label: Gently explain: 'Goldie died. Dead means her body stopped working and won't start again.'
choices.feedback: It's never too late to be clear.

b.text: She asks, 'Will you die too?' What do you say?

choices.label: 'Most people die when they are very, very old. I plan to be here to look after you for a long, long time.'
choices.feedback: Honest and reassuring.

choices.label: 'Never! I'll never die.'
choices.feedback: Well-meant, but not true – later it can shake trust. Reassure without promising the impossible.

d.text: She wants to do something for Goldie. What could you do?

choices.label: Bury Goldie in a pot and plant a flower; share memories
choices.feedback: Simple rituals help children grieve.

choices.label: Tell her to stop being sad
choices.feedback: Sadness is healthy. Let her feel and talk about it.

end.text: Clear words, honest reassurance, small rituals and permission to feel sad help children cope with loss.

story.title: The word from the school bus

scenes.text: In Delhi, Rohan (6) comes home from the school bus and says a swear word he heard from older boys.
His mother, Seema, feels the urge to shout. Instead she asks calmly, 'Where did you hear that word? Do you know what it means?'
Rohan shrugs. 'The big boys laughed when they said it.'
Seema explains: 'It's a rude word that people use to hurt or insult someone. We don't use it in our family. If you hear a word and wonder, ask me – you won't be in trouble.'

steps.title: Why children repeat bad words
steps.body: Young children copy words for the **reaction** they get, to sound grown-up, or because they don't know the meaning. A big shocked reaction makes the word more powerful and more fun to repeat.

steps.title: A calm script
steps.body:
1. **Stay calm** (neutral face).
2. **Ask:** 'Where did you hear it? What do you think it means?'
3. **Explain simply, without repeating or defining graphic meanings:** 'That's a rude word. It's used to hurt people or to talk about bodies in a disrespectful way.'
4. **State the family rule:** 'We don't use that word.' Offer alternatives for big feelings: 'Oh no!', 'I'm so angry!', a silly made-up word.
5. **Thank them for asking** – you want to be their source of answers.

steps.title: Words that hurt groups of people
steps.body: If a child repeats a slur about caste, religion, skin colour, disability, gender or sexuality, explain that it's a word used to **put people down for who they are**, that it causes real hurt, and that in your family everyone is treated with respect.

steps.title: When it's more than a word
steps.body: If a young child uses sexual words together with detailed knowledge of sexual acts, ask gently where they learned it. It may come from exposure to adult content or from abuse; seek advice (paediatrician, child psychologist, **Childline 1098**). Check device and internet settings at home.

steps.title: Model it
steps.body: Children copy what they hear at home. If you swear at traffic, they will too. A quick 'Oops, that was a rude word, I'm sorry' teaches repair.

steps.title: True or false?
steps.body: Check your instincts.

statements.s: A huge shocked reaction makes a bad word less interesting.
statements.why: Big reactions often make children repeat words more.

statements.s: Asking 'Where did you hear that?' helps you understand the situation.
statements.why: It tells you the source and what they know.

statements.s: You must give a detailed definition of every swear word.
statements.why: A simple, non-graphic explanation is enough.

statements.s: Offering alternative words for big feelings helps.
statements.why: Children need ways to express anger.

statements.s: Detailed sexual knowledge in a 5-year-old can be a reason to seek advice.
statements.why: It may indicate exposure or abuse.

scenes.text: At a metro station in Bengaluru, Zara (4) loudly asks, 'Why is that man in a chair with wheels?'
Her father, Imran, feels embarrassed – but the man smiles.
Imran says, 'Some people's legs don't work in the way ours do, so a wheelchair helps them move. He's going to work, just like us.'
The man says, 'That's right! And it's very fast.' Zara waves. 'Bye!'

steps.title: Curiosity, not rudeness
steps.body: Young children notice differences – skin colour, wheelchairs, hearing aids, hijabs and turbans, size, two dads or a single mum – and ask out loud. They're not being rude; they're learning. **Hushing them** teaches that difference is shameful.

steps.title: What to say
steps.body:
- **Disability:** 'His legs work differently, so a wheelchair helps him get around.' 'She uses her hands to talk – it's called sign language.'
- **Skin colour:** 'People have different skin colours – it comes from something called melanin and from their families. Everyone's skin is good skin.'
- **Families:** 'Some families have a mum and dad, some one parent, some grandparents, some are adopted. What makes a family is that they love and care for each other.'
- **Clothes and faith:** 'He wears a turban because of his religion, Sikhism. Your Nani wears a bindi.'

steps.title: Teach respectful habits
steps.body:
- Talk **about** differences at home, through books and friends.
- Teach: we don't point, stare or touch someone's wheelchair or hair without asking.
- It's okay to say hello! People with differences are people first.
- Avoid words like 'normal' vs 'not normal' – say 'different from us'.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- 'Shh! Don't look!' (teaches fear).
- 'We don't see colour' (children do; they need words for it).
- Laughing along with jokes about appearance, caste or religion.

steps.title: Sunlight is a mix
steps.body: Sunlight looks white, but it is a **mix of all the rainbow colours**: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. A rainbow, a prism or a glass of water can split them apart.
steps.say: Sunlight looks white, but it is a mix of all the rainbow colours: red, orange, yellow, green, blue, indigo and violet. A rainbow, a prism or a glass of water can split them apart.

steps.title: Air scatters blue
steps.body: Air is made of tiny, tiny bits we cannot see. When sunlight hits them, **blue light gets bounced (scattered) all over the sky much more than red light**. So when we look up, blue comes at us from everywhere – the sky looks blue!
steps.say: Air is made of tiny, tiny bits we cannot see. When sunlight hits them, blue light gets bounced (scattered) all over the sky much more than red light. So when we look up, blue comes at us from everywhere – the sky looks blue!

steps.title: Why sunsets are orange
steps.body: At sunrise and sunset, sunlight goes through much **more air** to reach us. Most of the blue gets scattered away on the way, so the light that reaches our eyes looks **orange and red**.

steps.title: Why brush?
steps.body: Tiny germs on our teeth love sugar. They make acid that can make **holes** (cavities) in teeth. Brushing removes the germs and food bits.

steps.title: How to brush
steps.body:
- Brush **twice a day** – morning and before bed.
- Use a **small, soft** toothbrush and a **pea-sized** blob of fluoride toothpaste (for ages 3–6).
- Brush **all sides** of every tooth – front, back and chewing tops – in small circles, for about **2 minutes**.
- **Spit out**, don't swallow the paste. Don't need to rinse a lot.
- A grown-up should help or check brushing until about 7–8 years old.

steps.title: Flat vs solid

steps.title: Five solid shapes

- **Sphere** – ball, laddoo, orange. Rolls in any direction. No flat faces.
- **Cube** – dice, ice cube. 6 square faces, all the same.
- **Cuboid** – brick, matchbox, tiffin box. 6 faces, some long.
- **Cylinder** – tin, pipe, candle. 2 circle faces; rolls and also stacks.
- **Cone** – ice-cream cone, birthday cap. 1 circle face and a point.

steps.title: Things to know by heart
steps.body:
- Your **full name**.
- Your parent's or carer's **full name**.
- A **phone number** (practise it as a song).
- Your **address** or area and city.

steps.title: If you get lost
steps.body:
1. **Stop** and stay where you are.
2. Look for a **safe helper**: a police officer, a shop worker at the counter, a security guard in uniform, or a mother with children.
3. Tell them your name and your parent's phone number.
4. **Do not go anywhere** with anyone – stay inside the shop or place.

**112** is India's emergency number for police, fire and ambulance. Call it if there is a **fire**, someone is **badly hurt** or **not waking up**, or someone is in **danger**. Say: what happened, where you are, your name. Stay on the phone. **Never call 112 as a joke** – real people need it.

steps.title: Traffic light colours
steps.body:
For cars: **Red = stop**, **Yellow/amber = get ready / slow down**, **Green = go**.

For walkers there is often a **red standing person** (wait) and a **green walking person** (cross with care).

steps.title: Stop, look, listen, think
steps.body:
1. **Stop** at the edge of the road (the kerb).
2. **Look right, look left, look right again.** (In India vehicles drive on the left, so the nearest traffic comes from your **right**.)
3. **Listen** for horns and engines.
4. **Think** – cross only when the road is clear.
5. **Walk** straight across – don't run, don't stop in the middle.

steps.title: Road rules for little ones
steps.body:
- **Always hold a grown-up's hand** near roads.
- Use **footpaths**, **zebra crossings**, **subways** or **foot-over bridges**.
- Never cross between **parked cars** – drivers can't see you.
- Never run after a ball onto the road.
- Wear bright clothes at night or on dark rainy days.

steps.title: The swimsuit rule
steps.body: Your **private parts** are the parts covered by your swimsuit or underwear: **chest**, **bottom**, and **penis and testicles** (boys) or **vulva and vagina** (girls). These are their real names – it's okay to say them.

steps.title: My body belongs to me
steps.body:
- My body belongs to **me**.
- Nobody should **touch**, **look at** or **take pictures** of my private parts.
- Nobody should ask me to touch **their** private parts.
- The only exceptions: a parent or carer helping me **wash or use the toilet**, or a **doctor or nurse** checking me **with my parent there**, to keep me healthy.

steps.title: I can say no to any touch
steps.body: Even a hug or kiss from a relative: if you don't want it, you can say 'No thank you' and give a **high five or wave** instead. Grown-ups should respect that.

steps.title: For parents
steps.body: Use a calm, ordinary voice, the same as teaching 'elbow'. Let your child decide about hugs and kisses with relatives – it teaches that *their* no matters. India's child helpline is **1098**; emergency **112**.

steps.title: Safe touches
steps.body: Safe touches make you feel **happy, cared for and safe**: a hug you want, holding hands to cross the road, a pat on the back, a high five, a doctor's check with your parent there.

steps.title: Unsafe touches
steps.body: Unsafe touches **hurt**, or make you feel **scared, confused, uncomfortable or yucky**: hitting, pinching, kicking, touching your private parts, or a touch someone says to keep **secret**.

steps.title: What to do: No, Go, Tell
steps.body:
1. **Say NO** loudly: 'No! Stop!'
2. **Go** – get away to a safe place.
3. **Tell** a trusted grown-up right away.

Even if you couldn't say no or get away, **telling** is always the right thing.

steps.title: Feelings are a warning bell
steps.body: If a touch gives you an 'uh-oh' feeling in your tummy, listen to it. You will **never be in trouble** for telling, even if the person is someone you know, someone in your family, or someone who gave you gifts.

steps.title: A surprise
steps.body: A **surprise** is something we keep quiet for a **short time** and then **everyone finds out** – and it makes people **happy**. Birthday gifts, a party, a cake.

steps.title: A secret
steps.body: A **secret** is something someone says you must **never tell**. If a secret makes you feel **worried, scared, sad or confused**, or it's about **touching**, **pictures** or someone **hurting** you – it is an **unsafe secret**. **Always tell** a trusted grown-up.

steps.title: Watch out for tricks
steps.body: Someone might give gifts, sweets or treats, or say 'Your parents will be angry' or 'Nobody will believe you', to make a child keep a secret. These are tricks. Grown-ups who care about you will **never** ask you to keep unsafe secrets.

steps.title: For parents
steps.body: Use the word **surprise** for nice things in your family and avoid asking children to keep 'secrets' from the other parent. Say often: 'You can tell me anything, and I will not be angry with you.'

steps.title: Never your fault
steps.body: If anyone touches you in an unsafe way, shows you private pictures or asks you to keep an unsafe secret, **it is never, ever your fault** – even if you said yes at first, took a gift, didn't say no, or it happened more than once. The grown-up or older child is responsible.

steps.title: Feelings after
steps.body: You might feel sad, scared, angry, confused or ashamed. These feelings are normal. Telling a trusted grown-up helps the feelings get smaller.

steps.title: Screens too
steps.body: If someone online or on a phone asks you for pictures of your body, shows you pictures of private parts, or says 'keep it secret' – **don't reply, close it, and tell** a trusted grown-up.

steps.title: For parents: if your child tells you
steps.body: **Stay calm**, believe them, thank them for telling, tell them it's not their fault, don't question them repeatedly or confront the person in front of them. Contact **Childline 1098** or **112** for help and guidance; India's POCSO Act protects children and requires such offences to be reported.

lessons.title: Private parts have names too

scenes.text: In Patna, Ravi (3) asks his father, 'What is this called?' while getting dressed.

steps.title: Correct names
steps.body:
Child-safety experts recommend teaching **correct names** for all body parts, just like 'elbow' or 'knee':

- Boys have a **penis** and **testicles**.
- Girls have a **vulva** (the outside) and a **vagina** (inside).
- Everyone has a **bottom** (and a **bottom hole**, the anus) and **chest/nipples**.

The **private parts** are the parts covered by underwear (and for girls later a swimsuit top).
steps.say: Child-safety experts recommend teaching correct names for all body parts, just like 'elbow' or 'knee': Boys have a penis and testicles. Girls have a vulva (the outside) and a vagina (inside). Everyone has a bottom (and a bottom hole, the anus) and chest/nipples. The private parts are the parts covered by underwear (and for girls later a swimsuit top).

steps.title: Why correct names?
steps.body: When children know the right words, they can **tell a grown-up clearly** if something hurts or if someone touches them. It also shows that bodies are normal – not something to be ashamed of.
steps.say: When children know the right words, they can tell a grown-up clearly if something hurts or if someone touches them. It also shows that bodies are normal – not something to be ashamed of.

steps.title: My body belongs to me
steps.body:
- My body belongs to me.
- My private parts are private.
- Nobody should touch them or ask to see them, except to keep me clean or healthy (with a trusted grown-up).
- If someone does, I **say no, go away, and tell** a trusted grown-up.
- It is **never my fault**.
steps.say: My body belongs to me. My private parts are private. Nobody should touch them or ask to see them, except to keep me clean or healthy (with a trusted grown-up). If someone does, I say no, go away, and tell a trusted grown-up. It is never my fault.

steps.title: For parents
steps.body: Say the names in a calm, everyday voice. Avoid nicknames that make the part sound shameful. Start a habit of daily 'tell me about your day' chats so telling you things feels normal. If you ever suspect abuse in India, call **1098** (Childline) or **112**.

steps.title: Signs of readiness (often 18 months–3 years)
steps.body:
- Stays dry for 1–2 hours or wakes dry after naps.
- Notices or tells you when nappy is wet or dirty.
- Can pull pants up and down (with help).
- Shows interest in the toilet or copying others.
- Can follow simple instructions.

Every child is different. Starting before the child is ready usually takes longer.
steps.say: Stays dry for 1–2 hours or wakes dry after naps. Notices or tells you when nappy is wet or dirty. Can pull pants up and down (with help). Shows interest in the toilet or copying others. Can follow simple instructions. Every child is different. Starting before the child is ready usually takes longer.

steps.title: Step-by-step plan
steps.body:
1. Get a potty or child seat with a step. Let the child sit on it clothed.
2. Use clear words: **wee (urine)** and **poo**.
3. Sit on the potty at regular times: after waking, after meals, before bath and bed.
4. Watch for signs (wriggling, holding) and say 'Let's go potty!'
5. Teach **wiping front to back** (especially for girls), flushing, and **washing hands with soap**.
6. Praise trying, not just success.

Teach wiping front to back (especially for girls), flushing, and washing hands with soap. 6. Praise trying, not just success.

steps.title: Common mistakes
steps.body:
- **Punishing or shaming** accidents – this causes fear and holding, which can lead to constipation.
- Starting during a big change (new baby, moving house).
- Expecting night dryness at the same time – night dryness often comes much later; bedwetting is common even at 5.

steps.title: When to ask a doctor
steps.body: If your child has pain while passing urine or stool, hard stools, blood, or was dry and suddenly starts having many accidents, talk to your paediatrician.
